summary: Phase 149O.1H.3 -- HATP Sub-Microsecond Timestamp Truncation Narrow Repair: repaired the narrow basis on which Phase 149O.1H.2 reopened B-149O.1H-1. Reproduced the defect directly against the unmodified pre-repair source: datetime.fromisoformat('2026-01-01T12:00:00.0000001+00:00').microsecond == datetime.fromisoformat('2026-01-01T12:00:00.0000009+00:00').microsecond == 0, and against the production module, _require_issued_at('2026-01-01T12:00:00.0000001Z') == _require_issued_at('2026-01-01T12:00:00.0000009Z') == '2026-01-01T12:00:00.000Z' -- both distinct raw strings accepted and canonicalized identically. Root cause: CPython's datetime.fromisoformat silently discards (never rejects) fractional-second digits past the sixth, and the millisecond-domain check (Phase 149O.1H.1) operates on datetime.microsecond, which is already lossy by the time that check runs. Repair strategy: validate raw lexical fractional-second precision BEFORE datetime.fromisoformat runs, per the narrow preferred strategy. Added a single new regex constant, _FRACTIONAL_SECONDS_RE = re.compile(r'\\.(\\d+)(?=Z$|[+-]\\d{2}:\\d{2}$)'), matching the raw fractional-second digit group immediately preceding the timestamp's Z/offset suffix, and a new helper, _reject_excess_fractional_precision(value, context=...), which raises InvalidProofSchemaError if that captured group exceeds 6 digits (the most Python's datetime can represent without truncation). This helper is called from _parse_iso_timestamp -- the sole call site both the parser (_build_proof_from_document -> _require_issued_at) and every constructor __post_init__ (_require_issued_at, call site unchanged) already share, so no second, drifting timestamp-validation path was introduced; B-149O.1H-2's shared-validator architecture is preserved. The pre-existing millisecond-domain rule (parsed.microsecond % 1000 != 0 -> reject) and the canonical renderer (_canonical_timestamp_string) are both textually and behaviorally unchanged. Post-repair verification: both the original millisecond-level collision (.0001Z/.0009Z, Phase 149O.1H.1's scope) and the new sub-microsecond collision (.0000001Z/.0000009Z, Phase 149O.1H.2's reopened scope) are now rejected via InvalidProofSchemaError, confirmed through both the parser and direct constructor paths. A full 7+-digit collision matrix (.0000001/.0000009, .0010001/.0010009, .1234561/.1234569, .9999991/.9999999) is rejected on both sides of each pair. A <=6-digit lexical/millisecond-domain separation matrix (.000000 accepted, .000001 rejected by the millisecond rule, .001000 accepted, .123000 accepted, .123456 rejected, .999999 rejected) confirms the lexical guard and the millisecond-domain rule operate as two independent layers, not one conflated rule. Offset timezone forms (+01:00, -05:00) with excess precision are rejected identically to the Z form; timezone equivalence for accepted values (12:00:00.001Z == 13:00:00.001+01:00 == 07:00:00.001-05:00) and distinctness for different milliseconds are both preserved. Parser/constructor equivalence was independently confirmed across the full precision matrix (no-fraction, 3-digit, 6-digit, 7-digit, mixed forms) -- both paths produce the identical accept/reject outcome for every case. Canonical bytes and SHA-256 digest for an already-accepted millisecond fixture (issued_at=2026-03-04T05:06:07.008Z) were independently recomputed and confirmed unchanged from the pre-repair rendering; no golden constant required updating. A bounded injectivity sweep over distinct accepted millisecond instants produced zero canonical-string collisions. Two historical-defect tests in the 149O.1H.2 suite (test_sub_microsecond_fractional_digits_are_silently_truncated_not_rejected, test_new_finding_sub_microsecond_collision_reproduced), which previously asserted the pre-repair (defective) acceptance behavior as expected-current, were updated in place -- not deleted -- to assert the now-repaired rejection behavior, following the same historical-test-flip convention Phase 149O.1H.1 established for Phase 149O.1H's own tests; the pre-repair narrative is preserved in this phase's docstrings, in git history, and in this document. A new authoritative regression suite, tests/test_phase_149o_1h_3_hatp_sub_microsecond_timestamp_truncation_repair.py, adds 57 tests covering the historical collision pair, the original millisecond-domain collision pair, the fractional-digit-length matrix (0 through 12 digits), the <=6-digit lexical/millisecond-domain separation matrix, short-fractional-form instant equivalence, the 7+-digit collision matrix, timezone-suffix coverage, timezone equivalence, parser/constructor equivalence, canonical-bytes/digest stability, injectivity, raw-losslessness, and regressions for boolean proof_version, invalid repository_id, invalid digests, malformed commit SHA, empty identifiers, AG3/AG5 family mismatch, closed-schema unknown fields, and duplicate JSON keys. Files changed: src/pcae/core/human_approval_trusted_provenance.py (production, 1 file, ~20 lines added), tests/test_phase_149o_1h_2_hatp_proof_models_canonical_serialization_independent_reverification.py (2 tests updated in place), tests/test_phase_149o_1h_3_hatp_sub_microsecond_timestamp_truncation_repair.py (new, 57 tests), docs/PHASE_149O_1H_3_HATP_SUB_MICROSECOND_TIMESTAMP_TRUNCATION_REPAIR.md (new), PROJECT_STATUS.md, CHANGELOG.md, plus task-lifecycle files. Zero other src/pcae/** production files, zero docs/contracts/** files touched -- UNRELATED = 0. B-149O.1H-1 REPAIRED (implementation verdict -- raw timestamp domain is now lossless before canonicalization: any issued_at carrying more than 6 fractional digits is rejected before datetime.fromisoformat runs; any value that survives the lexical guard is then subject to the unchanged millisecond-domain rule; a follow-up independent re-verification phase, 149O.1H.4, is required before this may be considered closed for governance purposes). B-149O.1H-2, F-149O.1C-1, F-149O.1C-2, B-149O.1F-1, B-149O.1R-1, B-149O.1R-2 all unaffected/unchanged. B-149O-1 through B-149O-4 remain OPEN. HATP production remains NOT READY -- Wave 4 verification engine, signature verification, provider attestation verification, trusted-signer resolution, human-presence verification, real FIDO2/PIV providers, Class-B deployment, and RAE/HATP integration remain entirely unimplemented. A structurally valid HATP proof still does NOT imply HATP VALID. Runtime remains Observed, maximum capability remains observe, execution availability remains unavailable.
